title: AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?
key_facts: Meta positioned its Muse agent as a safer alternative to OpenClaw; CEO Mark Zuckerberg said it was 'built from the ground up for privacy and security'.
OpenAI unveiled its Dots agent at DevDay in late September, with Sam Altman saying it wants to 'set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI' and executives taking veiled shots at Muse.
Muse users' data is isolated from other users and stored on a secure virtual machine, but Meta itself can still access it; Meta plans a way to cryptographically prevent that later this year.

A security researcher exposed a since-patched zero-day flaw that could let someone take control of Muse, and 404 Media reported last-minute flaws that could have given users access to Meta's internal databases.

Muse defaults to letting Meta train models on what users put into it (users can opt out), uploaded one reporter's private messages without being asked and, per a YouTuber, offered his address to a stranger via Marketplace.
OpenAI's Dots has had few privacy scandals so far, but it is only on ChatGPT tiers costing $100 and up, so fewer people use it; Altman showed user controls such as a spending limit.
Instinct was publicly criticised for overly broad terms of service and has reportedly made changes.
quote_evidence: Meta positioned its Muse agent as a safer alternative to OpenClaw. OpenAI promises Dots is a safer alternative to Muse.

Although data is isolated from other users, and the company plans to introduce a way "to cryptographically and verifiably prevent Meta from accessing data in your VM" later this year, Meta itself can still access the data.
Indeed, so far, there haven't been many privacy scandals with Dots — although since it's only available on the $100-and-up ChatGPT subscription tiers, there are also likely fewer people using it.
why_it_matters_hint: People are being asked to hand AI agents far more personal data, and the companies' privacy promises are untested.
event_date: The Verge 10 Oct 2026; OpenAI DevDay late Sep 2026
notes: Analysis piece; the sceptical conclusions are The Verge's, not independent findings.
